procedural_history.impugned_order: Second detention order passed on August 20, 1969, under s. 14(1) of the Jammu & Kashmir Preventive Detention Act, 1964.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: Original Jurisdiction: Writ Petition No. 168 of 1969 filed under Article 32 of the Constitution of India, seeking a writ in the nature of habeas corpus.

directions: He is, therefore, ordered to be released forthwith unless required in some other connection.

issue.issue_text: Whether a second detention order could be validly made without fresh material, as contemplated by s.14(2) of the Detention Act.

facts: A person (the detenu) was held under a detention order.
This first order was revoked on August 20, 1969.
On the very same day, a fresh order of detention was passed against the same person.
The detenu challenged this second detention order, arguing it was invalid because it was not based on any new material.
law: The case centered on the interpretation of Section 14(2) of the Jammu & Kashmir Preventive Detention Act.

Section 14(2) states that a fresh detention order can be made against the same person after a previous order is revoked or expires, but only "where fresh facts have arisen after the date of revocation or expiry".

The Court relied on its own binding precedent from cases like *Hadbandhu Das v. District Magistrate, Cuttack*, which interpreted a nearly identical provision and held that a second detention order requires additional or fresh material.
application: The Court interpreted the language of Section 14(2) as a mandatory requirement, making it "incumbent upon the Government to base the detention on some fresh facts."
It reasoned that once a detention order is revoked, the person is entitled to their liberty. To place them in "a second jeopardy" by detaining them again, there must be new grounds for doing so.

The Court found that since the second order was issued on the same day as the revocation of the first, and while the person was still in custody, there could not have been any "fresh facts" to justify the new order.

The Court distinguished an earlier case that allowed a second detention on the same grounds by noting that the law in that case (the Defence of India Rules) did not contain a provision equivalent to Section 14(2).
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the second order of detention was invalid because it was not based on any additional or fresh material, as explicitly required by Section 14(2) of the Act. Therefore, the detenu was entitled to be released.

issue.issue_text: Whether the non-service of the order of detention as well as the order under s.8 (2) upon the detenu is fatal to his continued detention.

facts: The petitioner challenged his detention on two main grounds.
The first ground was that a second detention order could not be made without fresh material, as required by s.14(2) of the Act.
The second ground was the specific issue in question: that the non-service of the detention order was fatal to his continued detention.
application: The Supreme Court chose to first examine the petitioner's first argument regarding the need for fresh material for a second detention order.
The Court agreed with the petitioner on this first point, finding that the second detention order was invalid because it was not based on any additional or fresh facts as required by s.14(2).
This conclusion was sufficient on its own to grant the petitioner relief.
reasoning.conclusion: Because the Court decided that the detenu was entitled to be released based on the first argument (the lack of fresh material), it explicitly stated that it was not necessary to examine or make a decision on the second issue regarding the non-service of the detention order.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a second detention order could be validly made without fresh material, as contemplated by s.14(2) of the Detention Act.
appellant_arguments: The second detention order could not be validly made except on some fresh material, as contemplated by s.14(2) of the Detention Act.
The government is required to base a new detention on fresh facts, not on the old facts from a previously revoked detention order.
respondent_arguments: A fresh detention order could be passed on the same facts, citing the precedent of Jagdev Singh v. State of Jammu & Kashmir.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the non-service of the order of detention as well as the order under s.8 (2) upon the detenu is fatal to his continued detention.
appellant_arguments: The non-service of the order of detention as well as the order under s.8(2) upon the detenu is fatal to his continued detention.
respondent_arguments: The gist of the orders was orally communicated to the detenu, implying this was sufficient.

cases.case_name: Unnamed case from All India Reporter
cases.principle: The clearest implication of Section 13(2) of the Preventive Detention Act is that after the revocation or expiry of a previous detention order, no fresh order may be issued on the same grounds. Fresh facts must be found for a new detention order.

cases.case_name: Kshetra Gogoi v. State of Assam
cases.principle: It affirmed the view that due to s. 14(2) of the J&K Act or the corresponding s. 13(2) of the Preventive Detention Act, it is incumbent upon the Government to base a fresh detention order on fresh facts, not the old facts on which a prior detention was ordered.

cases.case_name: Mohd. Shafi and Mohd. Yaqub v. State of Jammu & Kashmir
cases.citation: Writ Petition 183 of 1969, decided on October 17, 1969
cases.principle: It affirmed the view that due to s. 14(2) of the J&K Act or the corresponding s. 13(2) of the Preventive Detention Act, it is incumbent upon the Government to base a fresh detention order on fresh facts, not the old facts on which a prior detention was ordered.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: After a detention order is revoked or expires, a new detention order cannot be issued based on the same grounds on which the previous order was made; there must be fresh or additional facts to justify the new order.
obiter: A prior case that allowed a fresh detention order on the same grounds is distinguishable if it was decided under a different statute that did not contain a provision requiring fresh facts for a new order.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: In other words, the revocation or expiry of the previous order cannot lead ipso facto to a revival of the detention by the passing of a fresh order, because a person who is entitled to his liberty can only be put in a second jeopardy when there are additional or fresh facts against him. If the section had not spoken of t4e fresh facts, the matter might have been different, because, then, the courts would have been required to see whether there was any curb upon the power of the government to detain a person a second time after his release on the self-same material.
legal_tests_applied: The clearest implication of Sec,tion 13 ( 2) is that after revocation or expiry of the previous order, no fresh order may issue on the grounds on which the order revoked or expired had been made.
why_appellant_lost: The respondent's reliance on the precedent of Jagdev Singh v. State of Jammu & Kashmir was rejected because the statute in that case lacked a provision equivalent to s.14(2) of the Jammu & Kashmir Act, which explicitly requires fresh facts for a new detention order. The court stated: 'There was, however, no section equivalent ta ' s.13(2) of the Preventive Detention Act or s.14(2) of the Jammu & Kashmir Act in the Defence of India Rules under which that detention had proceeded.· This is sWlicient to distinguish the earlier case.'
why_respondent_won: The court followed a binding 'string of cases' which established that under s.14(2) of the Act, the government is required to base a new detention order on fresh facts, not the old facts from a previously revoked order. The court held: 'the enactment of s.14(2) of the Act or the corresponding section 13(2) of the Preventive Detention Act, 1950, makes it incumbent upon the Government to base the deten- tion on some fresh facts and not the old facts on which the dete.1- tion was once ordered but the revocation of the order took place. This view is binding upon us and applies in the present case.'
policy_considerations: A person who is entitled to his liberty can only be put in a second jeopardy when there are additional or fresh facts against him.
